learning_experiences: watch virtual or a demonstration of pushing and pulling activities in physical activities,
demonstrate pushing and pulling activities,
practise pushing and pulling activities,
sing songs while pulling and pushing,
play games using pulling and pushing skills by observing safety.
key_inquiry_questions: How can pulling and pushing skills be applied at home?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Digital literacy: the learner manipulates digital devices to watch clips showing pushing and pulling activities.
Self-efficacy: the learner appreciates their ability to demonstrate and practise pushing and pulling successfully.
sub_strands.values:
Unity: the learner cooperates with others as they perform pushing and pulling activities.
Respect: the learner portrays positive regard for self and others as they practise pushing and pulling activities.
sub_strands.pcis: Safety: The learner individually observes safety while playing games involving pushing and pulling.
sub_strands.links: Mathematical activities: the learner counts while pulling and pushing.

outcomes.text: identify pushing and pulling in physical activities for space and body awareness
perform pulling and pushing activities for flexibility
enjoy pushing and pulling for strength and flexibility

skills.name: Tell pushing from pulling in physical activities
skills.mastery: The child says pushing moves something away from the body (a wheelbarrow, a door, a friend's back in a pushing game) and pulling brings it towards the body (a rope in tug of war, a bucket from a well), sorts everyday and game actions into the two, and says why players keep their own space and push or pull without jerking. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, read aloud to the child where needed, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G3.RUBRIC.1.1), never as a phone question: b) perform pulling and pushing activities for flexibility.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
spot the mistake in a friend's answer

prerequisites.reason: Moving the body in named directions (Grade 2 turning) comes before moving objects towards and away from the body. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.
Moving along a straight line from a point (Grade 3 Maths) is what a push or a pull does to an object. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Calls bringing a bucket up from a well a push.

example.question: A girl brings a bucket of water up from a well with a rope. Is she pushing or pulling?

misconceptions.cause: The child links pushing with any hard work using the arms.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "pushing" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask: is the bucket coming towards her or going away from her?
misconceptions.feedback: The bucket comes towards her, so she is pulling.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says a wheelbarrow being moved along is pulled because it moves forward.

example.question: A boy moves a wheelbarrow in front of him. Is he pushing or pulling?

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks moving forward always means pulling.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "pulling" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Push a chair across the floor, then pull it, and say where the chair is each time.
misconceptions.feedback: The wheelbarrow goes away from his body in front of him, so he pushes it.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks tug of war is a pushing game.

example.question: In tug of war, what do the two teams do with the rope?

misconceptions.cause: Both teams lean hard, so the child sees a pushing contest.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "push it" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Hold a rope with a partner and pull it gently towards yourself.
misconceptions.feedback: In tug of war each team pulls the rope towards itself.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a sudden jerk is the best way to win a pulling game.

example.question: In a pulling game, what is the safe way to pull?
example.correct_answer: pull steadily and let go only when the teacher says

misconceptions.cause: The child sees jerking as stronger and does not think of the other team falling.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "jerk the rope suddenly" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show how a sudden jerk makes a partner fall, using a soft toy.
misconceptions.feedback: Pull steadily. A sudden jerk can make someone fall and get hurt.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: watch videos/pictures to recognise how to mix colour by spraying and blowing technique,
spray colours randomly using recyclable old brushes/improvised brushes and clean the hands after the activity,
mix the colour by blowing randomly using straws and a biro pen tube among others while observing safety,
draw and colour a simple composition using regular and irregular shapes,
paint a picture creatively for expression,
collaboratively, display their work for peer feedback.
key_inquiry_questions: Why is it important to clean the brush after painting?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Digital Literacy: the learner watches videos with peers to recognises how to mix colours by using the spraying and blowing technique.
Creativity and Imagination: the learner explores colours mixing techniques in painting.
sub_strands.values:
Unity: the learner respects others’ opinions while talking about their own and peers' pictures.
Social justice: the learner shares resources and responsibilities equitably while mixing coloured water paints.
sub_strands.pcis: Health promotion issues: the learner cleans the working area and washes hands after spraying paint.
sub_strands.links: Environmental Activities: the learner takes care of hygiene by cleaning their hands after painting.

outcomes.text: identify colour mixing for familiarity
mix colours using spraying and blowing techniques
draw a picture using regular and irregular shapes
create a painting for self-expression
value drawing and painting for expression

skills.name: Name the colours made by mixing two colours, and the spraying and blowing techniques
skills.mastery: The child names the secondary colour each pair of primaries makes (red and yellow make orange, blue and yellow make green, red and blue make purple), says that in spraying paint is flicked from an old brush and in blowing a drop of thin paint is blown with a straw so the colours run into each other, and says why brushes and hands are washed after painting. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, read aloud to the child where needed, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G3.RUBRIC.1.1), never as a phone question: b) mix colours using spraying and blowing techniques; d) create a painting for self-expression.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
spot the mistake in a friend's answer

prerequisites.reason: Painting with a brush (Grade 2) comes before mixing paint by spraying and blowing. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.
Knowing paints, brushes and sponges (Grade 1) is the start of colour work. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.

skills.name: Tell regular from irregular shapes in a picture
skills.mastery: The child names the regular shapes (circle, square, triangle, rectangle) in a picture, says that irregular shapes have no fixed form (a leaf, a cloud, a stone, a puddle), and points out both kinds in a simple drawing such as a house with a tree. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, read aloud to the child where needed, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G3.RUBRIC.1.1), never as a phone question: c) draw a picture using regular and irregular shapes.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
spot the mistake in a friend's answer

prerequisites.reason: Naming the basic shapes (Grade 3 Maths) is how regular shapes are picked out in a picture. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.
Painting regular shapes with a brush (Grade 2) comes before drawing a picture from regular and irregular shapes. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Says blue and yellow make brown or purple.

example.question: What colour do blue and yellow make when mixed?

misconceptions.cause: The child guesses from the colours they like or has mixed too many colours at once and got brown.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "purple" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Mix one drop of blue into yellow in front of the class.
misconceptions.feedback: Blue and yellow make green.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says red and yellow make pink.

example.question: What colour do red and yellow make?

misconceptions.cause: Pink is the light red the child knows best, so it is the first colour named.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "pink" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Mix red and yellow, then mix red and white, and compare the two.
misconceptions.feedback: Red and yellow make orange. Red and white make pink.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks mixing more colours always gives a brighter colour.

example.question: Ama mixes red, blue, yellow and green together. What colour will she get?

misconceptions.cause: More colours seems like more brightness to the child.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a bright rainbow colour" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Let the children mix all the colours in one cup and look.
misconceptions.feedback: Mixing many colours together makes a dull brown. Mix two at a time.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks blowing works best with a thick lump of paint.

example.question: For the blowing technique, what kind of paint do you use?
example.correct_answer: a drop of thin, watery paint

misconceptions.cause: Thick paint looks like more colour to the child.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a thick lump of paint" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Try blowing a thick blob and a watery drop with a straw.
misconceptions.feedback: Use a drop of thin paint. It runs when you blow it.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Calls a leaf a regular shape because it has a name.

example.question: Is a leaf a regular shape or an irregular shape?

misconceptions.cause: Everything with a name seems regular to the child.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "regular" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Draw a leaf and a square: does the leaf have a fixed form like the square?
misconceptions.feedback: A leaf is irregular. It has no fixed form like a square or a circle.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says a square standing on its corner is not a square.

example.question: A square is turned so it stands on one corner. Is it still a square?
example.correct_answer: yes, it is still a square

misconceptions.cause: Squares in books are always drawn sitting flat.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "no, it is a diamond" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Turn a paper square slowly and count its equal sides each time.
misconceptions.feedback: Turning a square does not change it. It is still a square.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Calls every four-sided shape a square.

example.question: A door has two long sides and two short sides. Which shape is it?

misconceptions.cause: Square is the first four-sided shape learnt.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a square" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Measure the sides of a door and of a square tile with string.
misconceptions.feedback: Two long sides and two short sides make a rectangle.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Draws clouds and stones only as circles because they are roundish.

example.question: Which shape is a cloud usually: a circle or an irregular shape?

misconceptions.cause: The child uses the nearest shape name for anything round.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a circle" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Go outside and trace the edge of a cloud or a stone with a finger.
misconceptions.feedback: Clouds and stones have bumpy, irregular shapes, not true circles.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

content_topics: Short and long sounds (taa-aa-aa-aa taa-aa, taa and ta-te )
learning_experiences: sing simple familiar songs for familiarisation of short and long sounds used in creating their rhythmic patterns,
listen to or watch live or recorded performances of simple songs and clap their rhythmic patterns,
use short and long sounds to create simple rhythmic patterns using body percussion or a percussion instrument,
provide rhythmic accompaniment to familiar songs using body percussion or a percussion instrument,
explore virtual sources to identify random and an all over patterns,
print a random pattern alternating colours to suggest rhythm, using
- a leaf
- block (banana stalk, maize cob, among others).
key_inquiry_questions: How can rhythms be created?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Creativity and imagination: the learner creates simple rhythmic patterns using short and long sounds.
Self-efficacy: the learner confidently plays rhythmic accompaniment to familiar songs.
sub_strands.values:
Responsibility: the learner takes care of the digital devices as they record the rhythmic chant performances for future use.
Respect: the learner gives a chance to peers as they take turns to recite short and long sounds using French rhythm names.
sub_strands.pcis: Social cohesion: the learner portrays team spirit as they work with peers to create rhythms using short and long sounds on a percussion instrument or body percussion.
sub_strands.links: Mathematical Activities: the learner applies knowledge and skill of counting to maintain the beat as they accompany songs with rhythmic accompaniment.

outcomes.text: identify different sound durations in simple songs
create a simple rhythmic pattern using long and short sounds
improvise rhythmic accompaniment to simple songs using long and short sounds
make a random repeat pattern using found objects
appreciate creating rhythms and patterns

skills.name: Tell long sounds from short sounds in a simple song
skills.mastery: The child says how long each French rhythm name lasts (ta-te is two short sounds in one beat, taa one beat, taa-aa two beats, taa-aa-aa-aa four beats), picks the longer and the shorter of two sounds in a known song, and matches clapped words to their rhythm names (Ke-nya is ta-te; the held 'sun' of a song is taa-aa). Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, read aloud to the child where needed, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G3.RUBRIC.1.1), never as a phone question: b) create a simple rhythmic pattern using long and short sounds; c) improvise rhythmic accompaniment to simple songs using long and short sounds.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
spot the mistake in a friend's answer

prerequisites.reason: Clapping the rhythm of simple words (Grade 2) is where long and short sounds are first felt. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.
The ways of making rhythm (Grade 2) are how long and short sounds are performed. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.

skills.name: Say what a random repeat pattern is
skills.mastery: The child says a random repeat pattern repeats the same print (a leaf, a bottle top, a cut potato) many times placed anywhere on the paper, unlike a regular pattern in straight rows, and names found objects that make good prints. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, read aloud to the child where needed, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G3.RUBRIC.1.1), never as a phone question: d) make a random repeat pattern using found objects.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
spot the mistake in a friend's answer

prerequisites.reason: Printing shape patterns (Grade 2) is the same printing used for a random repeat pattern. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.
Continuing a pattern of shapes (Grade 2 Maths) is the regular pattern a random repeat is compared with. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks ta-te is longer than taa because it has two syllables.

example.question: Which takes longer: ta-te or taa?
example.correct_answer: they take the same time, one beat

misconceptions.cause: Two syllables sound like more to the child.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "ta-te" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Walk one step to taa and one step to ta-te while clapping.
misconceptions.feedback: Ta-te and taa both last one beat. Ta-te has two short sounds in it.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says a loud sound is a long sound.

example.question: A drum is hit very hard once and stops quickly. Is it a long sound?
example.correct_answer: no, it is loud but short

misconceptions.cause: The child mixes loudness with length.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes, because it is loud" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Play one loud short sound and one soft long hum.
misconceptions.feedback: Loud is not long. A sound can be loud and short.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Counts taa-aa-aa-aa as two beats.

example.question: How many beats is taa-aa-aa-aa?

misconceptions.cause: The child counts the sound as one word plus a long ending.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "two" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Tap your knee for each "aa" while holding the sound.
misconceptions.feedback: Taa-aa-aa-aa lasts four beats.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Claps one clap per word instead of per syllable.

example.question: How many claps for "Ke-nya"?

misconceptions.cause: The child claps for whole words, as when counting words in English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "one" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Say the word slowly and clap each part: Ke, nya.
misconceptions.feedback: Clap each part of the word. Ke-nya has two claps.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a random repeat pattern must be printed in straight rows.

example.question: In a random repeat pattern, where do you place the prints?

misconceptions.cause: All patterns seen before were in rows.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "in straight rows only" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a row pattern and a random repeat side by side.
misconceptions.feedback: In a random repeat pattern the same print is placed anywhere on the paper.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Uses a different object for every print and calls it a repeat pattern.

example.question: Juma prints a leaf, then a bottle top, then a coin, all different. Is it a repeat pattern?
example.correct_answer: no; a repeat pattern uses the same print again and again

misconceptions.cause: The child hears "random" and thinks anything goes.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask: which print repeats? If none, it is not a repeat pattern.
misconceptions.feedback: A repeat pattern prints the same object many times.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Presses a dry object on paper and expects a print.

example.question: What must you do to a leaf before you print with it?

misconceptions.cause: The child has seen the print but not the inking step.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "nothing, just press it" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Press a dry leaf, then a painted leaf, and compare.
misconceptions.feedback: Put paint on the object first, then press it on the paper.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks only bought stamps can be used for printing.

example.question: Which can you use to print a pattern?
example.wrong_answer: only a stamp from a shop
example.correct_answer: found objects such as a leaf, a bottle top or a cut potato

misconceptions.cause: The child has seen printing only with shop stamps.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "only a stamp from a shop" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Collect objects from the school compound and test them.
misconceptions.feedback: Found objects like leaves and bottle tops make good prints.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

content_topics: Directions in Skipping (Forward, Backward, Right, Left
Pattern making (Straight line, curved, circular, zigzag).
learning_experiences: talk about skipping in different directions,
demonstrate skipping in different ways and directions,
practise skipping in different ways and directions with peers,
sing songs while skipping for enjoyment while making line patterns and shapes,
play games involving skipping activities with peers while observing safety,
share feedback about own and others performance in skipping.
key_inquiry_questions: Why are skipping activities interesting?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Creativity and Imagination: the learner pays attention to making patterns while skipping.
Self- efficacy: The learner individually skips confidently in different ways.
sub_strands.values:
Unity: the learner cooperates with peers while skipping.
Peace: the learner avoids hurting others by observing safety while playing games involving skipping.
sub_strands.pcis: Gender issues in education: the learner shows respect for gender equality while playing games in skipping with peers.
sub_strands.links: Mathematical Activities: the learner learns concepts of shapes and patterns.

outcomes.text: identify different ways of skipping in different directions
skip in different directions for skill acquisition
make patterns while skipping in different ways
appreciate skipping in different directions for balance and strength

skills.name: Name the directions and floor patterns of skipping
skills.mastery: The child names the directions of skipping (forward, backward, to the right, to the left), tells right from left by their own hands, and names the floor patterns a skipper can make (a straight line, a curve, a circle, a zigzag). Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, read aloud to the child where needed, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G3.RUBRIC.1.1), never as a phone question: b) skip in different directions for skill acquisition; c) make patterns while skipping in different ways.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
spot the mistake in a friend's answer

prerequisites.reason: The four directions of hopping and their floor patterns (Grade 2) are the same for skipping. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.
Telling right from left from a point (Grade 3 Maths) is needed to skip to the right or to the left. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up right and left, naming the teacher's right as their own.

example.question: Face the board and skip to your right. Which hand points the way?
example.correct_answer: my right hand, the one I write with if I am right-handed

misconceptions.cause: The child copies the teacher who faces them, so sides are mirrored.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "my left hand" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Stand with your back to the class and point right, then let children copy.
misconceptions.feedback: Your right is on your own right-hand side, not the side of the person facing you.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Calls a curved path a zigzag.

example.question: A path goes like a snake, smooth and bending. Is it a zigzag?

misconceptions.cause: Both paths change direction, so the child uses the word they like.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Chalk a zigzag with sharp corners and a curve with none.
misconceptions.feedback: A zigzag has sharp corners. A curve bends smoothly.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks skipping backward means turning round and skipping forward.

example.question: What does skipping backward mean?
example.correct_answer: keep facing the front and move backwards

misconceptions.cause: The child turns round to see where they are going.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "turn round and skip forward" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Put a mark in front and keep your eyes on it while moving back.
misconceptions.feedback: Skipping backward means you keep facing the front and move back.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a circular pattern means spinning on the spot.

example.question: Skip in a circular pattern. What do you do?
example.correct_answer: skip along the line of a big circle on the ground

misconceptions.cause: Circle and spinning both go round.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "spin round on the spot" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Draw a big circle and skip along its edge.
misconceptions.feedback: A circular pattern means moving round a big circle, not spinning on the spot.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: observe images of simple collage from actual or virtual environment for motivation to make a collage,
collect varied recyclable materials for making collage,
sort out materials to make the collage,
outline a simple picture to guide the pasting of materials,
collaboratively, paste different materials on the outlined forms,
show and talk about own and others’ collage, work.
key_inquiry_questions: What materials can be used to make a collage?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Communication and collaboration: the learner works collaboratively to paste the different materials on the outlined forms,
Self-efficacy: the learner expresses themselves about their artwork during display sessions
sub_strands.values:
Responsibility: the learner uses recyclable materials from the environment responsibly.
Love: the learner shows and talk about their own and others’ collage, works.
sub_strands.pcis: Life Skills: the learner develops self-awareness and self-esteem through display of their work and as they express their feelings, ideas and emotions.
sub_strands.links: Environmental Activities: the learner uses locally available materials emphasising the concept of use of recycled/reusable materials.

outcomes.text: identify a collage for familiarity
prepare materials for making the collage
create a collage for self-expression
appreciate using collage as an art of self-expression

skills.name: Say what a collage is and how its materials are prepared
skills.mastery: The child says a collage is a picture made by pasting pieces of different materials (coloured paper, cloth, seeds, leaves, feathers) onto a surface, says how materials are prepared (collect, clean and dry, cut or tear, sort by colour, make a flour or cassava paste), and tells a collage from a drawing or a painting. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, read aloud to the child where needed, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G3.RUBRIC.1.1), never as a phone question: c) create a collage for self-expression.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
spot the mistake in a friend's answer

prerequisites.reason: A mosaic and its materials and tools (Grade 2) are also pasted pieces; a collage uses pieces of different kinds and sizes. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.
Waste materials that can be reused (Grade 3 Environmental Activities) are many of the materials collected for a collage. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a collage is a coloured drawing.

example.question: Which picture is a collage?
example.correct_answer: a picture made by pasting pieces of paper, cloth and seeds

misconceptions.cause: All pictures look alike to the child at first.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a picture coloured with crayons" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Touch a collage: feel the pieces stuck on.
misconceptions.feedback: A collage is made by pasting pieces onto a surface.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a collage must use only one material, like a mosaic.

example.question: Can a collage use paper, cloth and seeds together?

misconceptions.cause: The Grade 2 mosaic used small pieces of one kind.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "no, only one material" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a collage with paper, cloth and feathers.
misconceptions.feedback: A collage can mix many materials.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Pastes leaves straight from the ground, wet and dirty.

example.question: What do you do to leaves before you paste them in a collage?

misconceptions.cause: The child does not know wet leaves rot and do not stick.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "paste them straight away" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Paste one wet leaf and one dry leaf and check the next day.
misconceptions.feedback: Clean and dry leaves first so they stick and last.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a collage cannot be made without shop glue.

example.question: You have no glue. What can you use to paste a collage?
example.correct_answer: a paste of flour or cassava and water

misconceptions.cause: The child has only seen glue from a shop.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "nothing, you cannot make it" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Mix flour and water together and test it.
misconceptions.feedback: A paste of flour and water sticks paper well.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

content_topics: Variation in rhythm, tempo (slow and fast), volume, (loud and soft), text, pitch,
learning_experiences: collaboratively listen to simple songs, noting variations in rhythm, volume, and speed in live or recorded performances and discuss them,
sing simple short songs and improvise variations in rhythm, tempo, volume, text and pitch,
use improvised pitched percussions such as bottles filled with water to different levels or two-tone wood blocks, to create melodic patterns,
collaboratively perform the created melodic patterns applying performance directions; slow/fast, soft/loud,
record the created melodies or play the melodies to peers for feedback.

Communication and Collaboration: the learner keenly listens to or watches live or recorded performances of simple songs and talks about the variations.
Creativity and Imagination: the learner creates melodic patterns from differently pitched objects.
sub_strands.values:
Respect: the learner provides feedback to peers’ performances using appropriate language.
Unity: the learner in groups researches from print and electronic media different simple ways of varying melodies.
sub_strands.pcis:
Safety and Security: the learner observes their safety as they create melodic patterns from differently pitched objects.
Social Cohesion: the learner portrays team spirit as they find out from the electronic media different simple ways of varying melodies.

outcomes.text: identify variations in a simple melodic pattern for aural skill development
create melodic patterns using improvised percussions
apply performance directions in performing simple songs
enjoy creating melodies using the variation technique

skills.name: Say how a simple melody has been varied
skills.mastery: The child hears a familiar tune sung again with one change and says what changed: faster or slower (tempo), louder or softer (volume), higher or lower (pitch), a new rhythm or new words. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, read aloud to the child where needed, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
spot the mistake in a friend's answer

prerequisites.reason: Hearing similar and different tunes (Grade 2) is the start of naming what has varied. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.
Putting new words to a tune (Grade 2) is one kind of variation. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.

skills.name: Follow the performance directions slow, fast, loud and soft
skills.mastery: The child says what each performance direction asks (slow, fast, loud, soft), that loud is not shouting and soft is not whispering out of tune, and follows the teacher's hand signs (hands wide for loud, close for soft) when told of them. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, read aloud to the child where needed, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G3.RUBRIC.1.1), never as a phone question: b) create melodic patterns using improvised percussions; c) apply performance directions in performing simple songs.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
spot the mistake in a friend's answer

prerequisites.reason: Hearing tempo and volume change in a melody comes before following directions to change them. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.
Performing a song with techniques (Grade 2) is where directions are followed. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Calls a louder version of a tune higher.

example.question: The class sings a song again, louder but on the same notes. What changed?

misconceptions.cause: In daily speech "turn it up" means both louder and higher.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "it got higher" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Sing the same note softly then loudly; then a low note and a high note.
misconceptions.feedback: Louder is volume. Higher is pitch. They are different.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says a faster tune is a higher tune.

example.question: A song is sung again more quickly. What changed?

misconceptions.cause: Fast songs often feel excited and high to the child.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the pitch went higher" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Sing a low tune quickly and a high tune slowly.
misconceptions.feedback: Faster is tempo. It does not make the notes higher.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a tune with new words is a new song.

example.question: The tune stays the same but the words change. Is it a new tune?
example.correct_answer: no, the same tune with new words

misconceptions.cause: The child remembers songs by their words.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes, a new tune" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Hum the tune without words, then sing both versions.
misconceptions.feedback: The tune is the same. Only the words changed.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says nothing changed when only the speed changed.

example.question: The song was sung slowly, then fast. Did anything change?
example.wrong_answer: no, it is the same song

misconceptions.cause: The child listens only for the words and tune.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "no, it is the same song" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: March to the song slowly and then fast.
misconceptions.feedback: The speed changed, so the tempo changed.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks singing loud means shouting.

example.question: The teacher says "loud". How do you sing?
example.wrong_answer: shout as hard as you can
example.correct_answer: sing strongly but still in tune

misconceptions.cause: Loud is the same as shouting in the playground.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "shout as hard as you can" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Sing loud, then shout, and listen for which keeps the tune.
misconceptions.feedback: Loud singing is strong and still in tune. Shouting is not singing.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Slows down when told to sing softly.

example.question: The teacher says "soft". What changes?
example.correct_answer: we sing more quietly at the same speed

misconceptions.cause: Soft and slow often go together in lullabies.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "we sing slower" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Clap a steady beat and sing softly over it without slowing.
misconceptions.feedback: Soft means quiet. The speed stays the same.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Gets louder when told to sing fast.

example.question: The teacher says "fast". What changes?

misconceptions.cause: Excitement makes the child sing faster and louder together.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "we sing louder" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Sing fast and soft, like a whisper race.
misconceptions.feedback: Fast means quick. It does not have to be loud.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Reads hands held close together as loud.

example.question: The teacher holds her hands close together. What does it mean?

misconceptions.cause: The child has not linked the size of the gap to the size of the sound.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "sing loud" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Open the hands wide and sing big; close them and sing small.
misconceptions.feedback: Hands close together mean soft. Hands wide apart mean loud.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

collect different coloured papers,
cut slits on a paper to make a paper loom,
cut paper strips of a different colour to the loom and dispose of waste responsibly,
interlace the strips by running over and under the slits on the paper frame to make paper mats in two colours,
experiment to make paper weaves with different colours,

Which other materials can be used for weaving?

outcomes.text: identify a plain paper weave for familiarity
create a plain paper weave to make
enjoy making paper mat using weaving

skills.name: Say how a plain paper weave is made
skills.mastery: The child says a plain paper weave is made by passing paper strips (the weft) over one and under one of the strips or slits of a base paper (the warp), that each new row starts the opposite way so a chequered pattern forms, and that two colours make the pattern show. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, read aloud to the child where needed, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G3.RUBRIC.1.1), never as a phone question: b) create a plain paper weave to make.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
spot the mistake in a friend's answer

prerequisites.reason: Plaiting a bracelet (Grade 2) already passes strands over and under each other. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.
Continuing a pattern (Grade 2 Maths) is how the alternate rows of a weave are planned. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Starts every row the same way (over first), so the strips slide out.

example.question: Row 1 started over. How should row 2 start?

misconceptions.cause: The child copies the row above exactly.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "over, the same as row 1" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Weave two rows the same way and lift the paper: the strip falls out.
misconceptions.feedback: Start each new row the opposite way to the one before.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Goes over two strips and under one in a plain weave.

example.question: In a plain weave, how does the strip go?

misconceptions.cause: The child skips strips by accident when the slits are close.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "over two, under one" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Say "over, under, over, under" aloud with each strip.
misconceptions.feedback: A plain weave goes over one and under one.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Cuts the slits right through to the edge of the base paper.

example.question: When you cut slits in the base paper, how far do you cut?
example.correct_answer: stop before the edge so the paper holds together

misconceptions.cause: The child cuts until the scissors stop.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "right to the edge" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show a base cut to the edge falling into strips.
misconceptions.feedback: Stop cutting before the edge so the base holds the warp.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the colours of the strips do not matter to the pattern.

example.question: Why use two colours in a paper weave?
example.correct_answer: so the over and under pattern shows

misconceptions.cause: The child has not seen a weave in one colour.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "it does not matter" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare a weave in one colour with one in two colours.
misconceptions.feedback: Two colours make the chequered pattern show.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

talk about how to sing in a round focusing on; posture, accuracy of tune, clarity of words, entries and keeping to own part,
sing own part in a round on a specific theme for skill development,
sing rounds with peers applying appropriate performance techniques,
collaboratively, take turns to sing own part in a round as others give feedback,
talk about the message in a round sung.
key_inquiry_questions: How are rounds sung?
sub_strands.core_competences:

Responsibility: the learner keeps to own part in a round performance.

sing own part in a round applying appropriate performance techniques

skills.name: Tell a round from other songs and say its message
skills.mastery: The child says that in a round every group sings the same song but starts at a different time, in two or three parts, and each group keeps to its own part; tells a round from a song sung all together (unison); says the message of a round they sing; and names the performance techniques (good posture, the right tune, clear words, starting on time). Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, read aloud to the child where needed, and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (CREA.G3.RUBRIC.2.1), never as a phone question: b) sing own part in a round applying appropriate performance techniques.
question_forms: pick the right answer
pick the right answer in a short story
spot the mistake in a friend's answer

prerequisites.reason: Singing a song with the right tune and clear words (Grade 2) is needed before keeping one part in a round. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.
Saying the message of a topical song (Grade 2) is how the message of a round is found. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the groups in a round sing different songs.

example.question: In a round, what do the groups sing?
example.correct_answer: the same song, starting at different times

misconceptions.cause: The sound is mixed, so the child thinks the songs differ.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "different songs" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Sing the round slowly with two groups, then each group alone.
misconceptions.feedback: In a round every group sings the same song, starting at different times.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a round starts with all groups together.

example.question: Do all groups start a round together?
example.correct_answer: no, one group starts, then the next joins later

misconceptions.cause: Most class songs start together.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Point to group 1 to start; point to group 2 after one line.
misconceptions.feedback: In a round each group starts later than the one before.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Switches to the other group's words when they hear them.

example.question: In a round you hear the other group singing a different line. What do you do?

misconceptions.cause: The child follows the loudest voices.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "join their line" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Practise with a hand over one ear, keeping your own words.
misconceptions.feedback: Keep to your own part even when you hear other words.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Calls a song sung all together a round.

example.question: The whole class sings the same words at the same time. Is that a round?
example.correct_answer: no, it is singing in unison

misconceptions.cause: Any group song seems a round to the child.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Sing a song in unison, then as a round, and compare.
misconceptions.feedback: Singing together at the same time is unison. A round starts at different times.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks galloping is hopping on one leg.

example.question: Is galloping the same as hopping?
example.correct_answer: no; in galloping both feet touch the ground, one leading

misconceptions.cause: Both are bouncy moves.

misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Swaps the leading foot every step.

example.question: In a gallop, which foot leads?
example.correct_answer: the same foot leads every time

misconceptions.cause: Walking and running swap feet, so the child does the same.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the feet take turns" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Put a ribbon on the leading foot and keep it in front.
misconceptions.feedback: In a gallop the same foot always leads.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Calls a skip a gallop.

example.question: Step-hop, step-hop, changing feet. Is that a gallop?

misconceptions.cause: Both moves have a quick rhythm.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Do a gallop and a skip to the same drum and compare.
misconceptions.feedback: Step-hop changing feet is a skip. A gallop keeps one foot leading.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks you cannot gallop to the side.

example.question: Can you gallop to the left?
example.correct_answer: yes, leading with the left foot

misconceptions.cause: Horses are seen galloping forward.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "no, only forward" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Face the board and gallop to the left, left foot leading.
misconceptions.feedback: You can gallop to the left or right with that foot leading.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a river is safe to cross after rain because the rain has stopped.

example.question: It rained heavily upstream. Is the river safe to cross now?
example.correct_answer: no, the river can rise and flow fast

misconceptions.cause: The child does not link rain far away with the river nearby.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes, the rain has stopped" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Show how water poured at one end of a gutter reaches the other end later.
misconceptions.feedback: After heavy rain a river can rise quickly. Do not cross it.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Says you should jump in to save a friend who has fallen into water.

example.question: Your friend falls into a dam. What should you do?
example.wrong_answer: jump in and pull them out
example.correct_answer: shout for an adult and throw something that floats

misconceptions.cause: The child wants to help and thinks being brave means jumping in.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "jump in and pull them out" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Role play: shout, find an adult, throw a jerrican or a stick.
misconceptions.feedback: Do not jump in. Shout for an adult and throw something that floats.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a child who can swim may swim alone in a river.

example.question: Can a child who can swim go into a river alone?

misconceptions.cause: Being able to swim feels like being safe.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes, if they can swim" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Talk about strong currents and hidden rocks.
misconceptions.feedback: Never go into a river alone, even if you can swim.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks pushing friends near water is just a game.

example.question: Is it all right to push a friend near a well as a joke?

misconceptions.cause: The child does not think of the result of a joke.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "yes, it is a game" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask: what could happen next?
misconceptions.feedback: Never push anyone near water. They could fall in.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Leaves the cover off a well after drawing water.

example.question: You finish drawing water from a well. What do you do?
example.wrong_answer: leave it open for the next person

misconceptions.cause: The child wants to be helpful to the next person.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "leave it open for the next person" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Ask: who else might walk past an open well?
misconceptions.feedback: Always cover a well after use so no one falls in.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Creative Activities teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.
